questions.q: In the SOCRATES mnemonic used for evaluating surgical pain, what does the letter R stand for?
questions.explain: In SOCRATES, R stands for Radiation, which tracks where pain spreads from its primary site (such as shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation). Exacerbating and relieving factors are covered under E.

open.q: In the SOCRATES pain assessment mnemonic, what clinical feature does the letter R represent?

questions.q: Which component of the surgical history specifically explores a patient's previous exposure to halothane or suxamethonium?
questions.explain: Past anaesthetic and surgical history identifies previous operations and any adverse anaesthetic reactions, such as halothane hepatitis or suxamethonium apnoea. Family history may also screen for inherited conditions like malignant hyperthermia.

open.q: Which section of a surgical clerkship specifically checks for previous complications with anaesthetic agents such as suxamethonium or halothane?

questions.q: Which anatomical landmark divides the abdomen into nine regions via the transpyloric plane horizontally?
questions.explain: The transpyloric plane (Addison's plane) lies at the lower border of the L1 vertebra, midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis. The transtubercular plane lies lower at L5.

open.q: At which vertebral level does the transpyloric plane cross the abdomen?

questions.q: What is the minimum threshold of serum bilirubin required for clinical jaundice to become visible in the sclera?
questions.explain: Clinical icterus becomes detectable in the sclera (rich in elastin, which has high affinity for bilirubin) once total serum bilirubin exceeds approximately 35 to 50 micromol/L (about 2 to 3 mg/dL). Normal serum bilirubin is below 17 micromol/L.

open.q: Over what serum bilirubin concentration in micromol/L does scleral jaundice become clinically apparent?

questions.q: Which clinical sign on general examination is characterized by loss of the normal angle between the nail plate and the proximal nail fold?
questions.explain: Digital clubbing begins with fluctuation of the nail bed and obliteration of Lovibond's angle (normally less than 160 degrees) between the nail plate and proximal nail fold. Koilonychia refers to spoon-shaped nails associated with iron deficiency.

open.q: What clinical nail finding is defined by obliteration of Lovibond's angle between the nail plate and proximal nail fold?

questions.q: In which position should a patient ideally be placed for a routine abdominal examination?
options: Supine with one pillow under the head and arms by the sides
Left lateral decubitus with hips flexed
Propped up at 45 degrees with hands behind the head
Prone with a pillow under the pelvis
questions.explain: Lying flat (supine) with a single pillow under the head and arms relaxed by the sides prevents tension in the rectus abdominis muscles. Placing hands behind the head or using multiple pillows tenses the anterior abdominal wall and obscures palpation.

open.q: How should a patient be positioned on the examination couch to achieve optimal relaxation of the anterior abdominal wall during routine inspection and palpation?
accept: Supine with one pillow and arms by the sides
Lying flat on the back with one pillow

questions.q: What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of Rovsing sign in acute appendicitis?
options: Direct irritation of the right psoas major muscle by a retrocaecal appendix
Retrograde displacement of colonic gas causing distension and peritoneal irritation in the right iliac fossa
Spasm of the right obturator internus muscle on internal rotation of the hip
Cutaneous hyperaesthesia in the T10 to T12 dermatomes
questions.explain: Palpating the left iliac fossa pushes gas and bowel contents retrogradely along the colon toward the caecum, stretching the inflamed appendix and irritating the parietal peritoneum in the right iliac fossa. Psoas and obturator signs involve direct muscular irritation.

open.q: Why does deep palpation of the left iliac fossa elicit pain in the right iliac fossa in a patient with a positive Rovsing sign?
accept: Retrograde movement of colonic gas distending the caecum and irritating the inflamed appendix
Displacement of colonic gas toward the right iliac fossa

questions.q: How is an enlarged spleen clinically distinguished from an enlarged left kidney on abdominal palpation?
options: A spleen is bimanually palpable and ballotable
A spleen has a palpable notch on its medial border and you cannot get above it
A spleen is resonant to percussion anteriorly due to overlying colon
A spleen moves medially rather than inferomedially on inspiration
questions.explain: An enlarged spleen enlarges inferomedially toward the right iliac fossa, possesses a characteristic medial notch, has a dull percussion note, and prevents the examiner from getting above it under the left costal margin. A kidney is ballotable, resonant anteriorly, and allows fingers to get above it.

open.q: State two classic palpation features that distinguish splenomegaly from a left renal mass.
accept: Presence of a splenic notch and inability to get above it
Notch on medial border and moves inferomedially on inspiration
Cannot get above it and dull to percussion

questions.q: Which percussion technique is used to confirm moderate ascites when flank dullness is detected?
questions.explain: Shifting dullness involves percussing from the resonant midline to the dull flank, rolling the patient onto the opposite side, waiting 10 to 30 seconds for free fluid to gravitate downward, and demonstrating that the previously dull flank has become resonant.

open.q: Name the bedside percussion manoeuvre used to confirm free peritoneal fluid after demonstrating flank dullness.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman with right upper quadrant pain suddenly catches her breath during deep inspiration while the examiner's fingers are pressed beneath the right costal margin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Inspiratory arrest upon palpation of the right subcostal region is a positive Murphy sign, indicating acute cholecystitis as the inflamed gallbladder descends during inspiration and strikes the examiner's hand. The sign is only valid if the same manoeuvre on the left side does not cause arrest.

open.q: A patient experiences sudden inspiratory arrest when the examiner palpates beneath the right costal margin during deep breathing. What is the eponymous sign and the condition it indicates?
accept: Positive Murphy's sign in acute cholecystitis

questions.q: Where is the anatomical surface marking of the deep inguinal ring?
options: 1.25 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
1.25 cm above and lateral to the pubic tubercle
4 cm inferolateral to the pubic tubercle
questions.explain: The deep inguinal ring lies 1.25 cm (half an inch) above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle). The femoral artery pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point, which is midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis.

open.q: Describe the surface landmark of the deep inguinal ring in relation to the inguinal ligament.
accept: 1.25 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
Half an inch above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
1 to 1.5 cm superior to the midpoint of the inguinal ligament

questions.q: During the deep ring occlusion test, after reducing an inguinal hernia, pressure is applied over the deep inguinal ring and the patient coughs. The bulge reappears medial to the occluding finger. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: Because a direct inguinal hernia protrudes directly through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle) medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, occluding the deep ring does not control it. An indirect hernia enters via the deep ring and stays controlled while pressure is maintained.

open.q: If a reduced groin hernia reappears medial to the examiner's finger during a deep inguinal ring occlusion test when the patient coughs, what type of hernia is present?

questions.q: In which anatomical position does the neck of a femoral hernia lie relative to the pubic tubercle?
options: Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Above and medial to the pubic tubercle
Above and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Directly posterior to the pubic symphysis
questions.explain: A femoral hernia emerges through the femoral ring below the inguinal ligament, placing its neck below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. In contrast, an inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle.

open.q: How is the neck of a femoral hernia located anatomically in relation to the pubic tubercle?
accept: Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle

questions.q: Which position is most commonly used in clinical practice to perform a routine digital rectal examination?
options: Left lateral (Sims) position with knees drawn up to the chest
Right lateral decubitus with legs fully extended
questions.explain: The left lateral position with hips and knees flexed (and buttocks near the edge of the couch) provides optimal comfort, exposure, and anatomical alignment for a right-handed examiner. Knee-elbow and dorsal lithotomy positions are alternatives in specific settings.

open.q: What is the standard patient position on an examination couch for performing a routine digital rectal examination?

questions.q: Which structure is normally palpable anteriorly during a digital rectal examination in an adult male?
options: Posterior surface of the prostate gland
questions.explain: Anteriorly in the male rectum, the smooth, bilobed posterior surface of the prostate gland with its median sulcus is palpable. The coccyx and sacrum are palpable posteriorly, and the ischial spines laterally.

open.q: Name the normal genitourinary organ felt along the anterior rectal wall during a digital rectal examination in a male patient.

questions.q: Which sign on breast inspection indicates lymphatic obstruction caused by an underlying breast carcinoma?
questions.explain: Peau d'orange (orange-peel skin) results from cutaneous lymphoedema caused by tumour cells blocking subdermal lymphatics, tethering the skin at hair follicles and sweat ducts. Montgomery tubercles are normal sebaceous glands on the areola.

open.q: What is the clinical term for dimpled, orange-peel appearance of breast skin caused by cutaneous lymphatic blockage?

questions.q: How do you clinically test whether a breast lump is fixed to the underlying pectoralis major muscle?
options: Ask the patient to press her hands firmly onto her hips while checking lump mobility
Ask the patient to raise both arms straight above her head
Pinch the overlying skin gently between thumb and index finger
Place the patient in the left lateral position
questions.explain: Pressing the hands onto the hips contracts the pectoralis major muscle. A lump tethered to the muscle fascia becomes less mobile along the axis of the muscle fibres (superomedial to inferolateral) when the muscle is tensed.

open.q: What manoeuvre is performed during breast palpation to contract the pectoralis major and assess deep fixation of a breast mass?
accept: Asking the patient to press her hands on her hips
Pressing hands against the iliac crests

questions.q: What is the primary diagnostic significance of asking a patient to swallow a sip of water during a neck examination?
options: A thyroid swelling moves upward on swallowing because it is enclosed by pretracheal fascia
A branchial cyst moves upward on swallowing due to carotid sheath attachment
A cystic hygroma empties completely during deglutition
A carotid body tumour stops pulsating on swallowing
questions.explain: The thyroid gland is invested by the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia, which is attached superiorly to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages and hyoid bone. Consequently, thyroid swellings and thyroglossal cysts elevate during swallowing.

open.q: Why does a thyroid swelling move upward when a patient swallows?
accept: Attachment of the pretracheal fascia to the larynx and hyoid bone
It is enclosed in the pretracheal fascia attached to the thyroid cartilage

questions.q: Which clinical sign is elicited by asking a patient with a retrosternal goitre to raise both arms above the head until they touch the sides of the face?
questions.explain: Pemberton sign is positive when raising the arms narrows the thoracic inlet (the cork-in-a-bottle effect), causing facial plethora, cyanosis, and engorgement of neck veins within a minute due to superior vena cava obstruction.

open.q: The clinical sign demonstrated when raising both arms over the head induces facial congestion and jugular venous distension in a patient with a retrosternal goitre.

questions.q: What is the standard site for palpating the dorsalis pedis artery pulse?
options: Just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon over the navicular and cuneiform bones
Two centimetres posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus
Deep in the midline of the popliteal fossa
questions.explain: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot just lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus over the tarsal bones. The posterior tibial pulse lies behind the medial malleolus.

open.q: Describe the anatomical landmark used to palpate the dorsalis pedis artery on the foot.
accept: Lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the dorsum of the foot
Just lateral to the EHL tendon
Dorsum of the foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus

questions.q: A 64-year-old smoker has a foot that turns pale when elevated to 30 degrees and becomes deep dusky red when hung over the side of the bed. What is this clinical finding called?
questions.explain: Pallor on elevation (Buerger's angle less than 20 to 30 degrees) followed by reactive hyperaemia (dependent rubor or sunset foot) on dependency indicates severe chronic lower limb arterial ischaemia.

open.q: In chronic lower limb arterial ischaemia, what is the name of the bedside test where elevating the leg produces pallor and lowering it produces reactive hyperaemia?

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the Brodie-Trendelenburg test in a patient with lower limb varicose veins?
options: To assess competence of the saphenofemoral junction and perforating veins
To rule out deep vein thrombosis in the calf
To measure the ankle-brachial pressure index
questions.explain: The Brodie-Trendelenburg test empties the superficial veins by leg elevation, applies pressure over the saphenofemoral junction, and observes whether varicosities refill rapidly on standing (incompetent perforators) or only upon releasing junctional pressure (saphenofemoral incompetence).

open.q: Which venous structures are evaluated for valvular competence using the Brodie-Trendelenburg test?
accept: Superficial venous valves and saphenofemoral junction

questions.q: Which clinical sign describes bluish periumbilical discolouration caused by retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking along the falciform ligament?
questions.explain: Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis seen in haemorrhagic pancreatitis or ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Grey Turner sign is bluish discolouration of the flanks, and Fox sign is bruising over the inguinal ligament.

open.q: Name the clinical sign characterized by bluish bruising around the umbilicus due to retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal bleeding.

questions.q: How does Carnett sign help differentiate abdominal wall pain from intra-abdominal visceral pain?
options: Tenderness increases or remains unchanged when the patient tenses the abdominal muscles
Tenderness completely disappears when the patient lifts their head off the pillow
Pain radiates to the right scapula upon deep palpation
Bowel sounds become high-pitched and tinkling on auscultation
questions.explain: When a patient lifts their head or straight legs to tense the rectus abdominis, tensed muscles guard underlying viscera so true intra-abdominal tenderness decreases, whereas pain originating in the abdominal wall (such as rectus sheath haematoma) persists or worsens.

open.q: What happens to localized abdominal tenderness in a positive Carnett sign when the patient tenses their abdominal wall muscles?

questions.q: During chest examination of a trauma patient, which combination of percussion and auscultation findings indicates a large haemothorax?
options: Stony dullness to percussion with absent breath sounds
Hyper-resonance to percussion with absent breath sounds
Woody dullness to percussion with bronchial breathing
Normal resonance with coarse inspiratory crackles
questions.explain: Fluid in the pleural space produces stony dullness on percussion and reduced or absent breath sounds with contralateral tracheal deviation if massive. Hyper-resonance with absent breath sounds characterizes a pneumothorax.

open.q: What percussion note and breath sound findings are classically present over a large haemothorax?
accept: Stony dullness and absent breath sounds
Stony dull percussion note and diminished or absent breath sounds
